style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare Greek transliterations in amp with Strong's carried in notes; em-dashes used sparingly; transliterations ASCII-normalized relative to the lexicon's spellings.
chapterNote: The letter closes with a prophet's thunder and a pastor's hands. First the thunder: a courtroom oracle against the rich who hoarded in the last days -- rotted riches, moth-eaten robes, corroded gold rising as a witness, and the defrauded harvesters' unpaid wages crying out until the cries reach the ears of the Lord of Hosts. To the oppressed brothers, the counsel is the farmer's: be long-patient until the coming of the Lord, as the farmer waits for the early and the latter rain; establish your hearts, stop groaning against each other -- the Judge is standing at the door -- and take the prophets and Job as your pattern, for the end of the Lord's dealings shows Him full of tender compassion. Above all, no oaths: let yes be yes and no be no. Then the pastor's hands: the suffering should pray, the cheerful sing, the sick call the elders for prayer and anointing in the name of the Lord; the prayer of faith will save the sick, sins confessed among brothers are sins healed, and the working prayer of a righteous man has great strength -- Elijah, a man of like nature to us, shut and opened the sky by it. The last word is a rescue: whoever turns a wanderer back from the error of his way saves a soul from death and covers a multitude of sins -- the letter ending in the very act it was written to perform.

1.text: Come now, you rich: weep and howl for the miseries that are marching toward you.
1.amp: Go to [age] now [nun], you rich men [plousios], weep [klaio] and howl [ololuzo -- wail aloud] for your miseries [talaiporia] that shall come upon [eperchomai] you.
1.notes: ololuzo (G3649) is the prophets' onomatopoeic wail (cf. Isaiah 13:6): James speaks here as Amos spoke, an oracle over the oppressing rich -- likely the unbelieving landholders of 2:6, addressed over the church's shoulder. The talaiporia (G5004) are already en route.

2.text: Your riches have rotted, and your fine garments have gone to the moths.
2.amp: Your riches [ploutos] are corrupted [sepo -- rotted], and your garments [himation] are motheaten [setobrotos].
2.notes: The perfect tenses are prophetic: the rot has, in God's court, already happened. sepo (G4595) is organic decay, and setobrotos (G4598) -- moth-eaten -- lands on the himation (G2440), the stored wealth of the ancient world (cf. Matthew 6:19-20, his Brother's identical audit).

3.text: Your gold and silver are corroded through, and their corrosion will stand as a witness against you and eat your flesh like fire. You have heaped up treasure in the last days.
3.amp: Your gold [chrusos] and silver [arguros] is cankered [katioo -- corroded, rusted through]; and the rust [ios] of them shall be a witness [marturion] against you, and shall eat [phago] your flesh [sarx] as it were fire [pur]. You have heaped treasure together [thesaurizo] for the last [eschatos] days [hemera].
3.notes: Gold cannot rust; James says theirs has -- hoarded wealth corrodes at a moral level chemistry cannot see. ios (G2447), the poison-word of 3:8, doubles as rust: it takes the marturion (G3142) stand, then turns executioner. thesaurizo in the eschatos hemera (G2078, G2250): stockpiling on the eve of the audit.

4.text: Look: the wages of the workers who mowed your fields, the pay you held back by fraud, are crying out, and the cries of the harvesters have entered the ears of the Lord of Hosts.
4.amp: Behold [idou], the hire [misthos -- the wages] of the labourers [ergates] who have reaped down [amao -- mowed] your fields [chora], which is of you kept back by fraud [apostereo -- defrauded, withheld], cries [krazo]: and the cries [boe] of them which have reaped are entered [eiserchomai] into the ears [ous] of the Lord [kurios] of sabaoth [sabaoth -- of Hosts, of Armies].
4.notes: Withheld misthos (G3408) was covenant crime with a same-day deadline (cf. Deuteronomy 24:14-15). The money itself krazo, cries from the strongbox like Abel's blood, and the harvesters' boe (G995) has already cleared security -- eiserchomai, entered -- into the ears of kurios sabaoth (G4519), the Lord of Armies, the title of the God who fights.

5.text: You have lived delicately on the earth and taken your pleasure; you have fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter.
5.amp: You have lived in pleasure [truphao -- luxuriated, lived delicately] on the earth [ge], and been wanton [spatalao -- lived in self-indulgence]; you have nourished [trepho -- fattened] your hearts [kardia], as in a day [hemera] of slaughter [sphage].
5.notes: truphao and spatalao (G5171, G4684): softness and self-indulgence as a settled career. The final image is the feedlot -- trepho (G5142), fattening the kardia -- while the hemera sphage (G4967), the day of slaughter, is already on the calendar. Cattle eat best the morning of the butchering.

6.text: You have condemned, you have murdered the righteous man, and he does not resist you.
6.amp: You have condemned [katadikazo] and killed [phoneuo] the just [dikaios -- the righteous one]; and he does not resist [antitasso -- set himself in array against] you.
6.notes: katadikazo then phoneuo (G2613, G5407): the courts of 2:6 running their full course -- legal murder, the poor man ground down to death. The dikaios does not antitasso (G498), the very verb of 4:6: he leaves the battle-array to God, who has taken the field against the proud already.

7.text: Be long-patient, then, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. Look how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, patient over it until it receives the early rain and the latter rain.
7.amp: Be patient [makrothumeo -- be long-tempered, suffer long] therefore, brethren [adelphos], unto the coming [parousia] of the Lord [kurios]. Behold [idou], the husbandman [georgos -- the farmer] waits [ekdechomai] for the precious [timios] fruit [karpos] of the earth [ge], and has long patience [makrothumeo] for it, until he receive [lambano] the early [proimos] and latter [opsimos] rain [huetos].
7.notes: The address turns back to the brothers: makrothumeo (G3114), the long temper that outlasts injustice, stretched unto the parousia (G3952) -- the royal word for a king's arrival. The georgos (G1092) is its picture: he cannot hurry the proimos or the opsimos rain (the autumn sowing-rain and the spring ripening-rain, cf. Deuteronomy 11:14), and he does not dig up the field to check.

8.text: You too be long-patient. Make your hearts firm, for the coming of the Lord has drawn near.
8.amp: Be you also patient [makrothumeo]; stablish [sterizo -- fix firmly, prop up] your hearts [kardia]: for the coming [parousia] of the Lord [kurios] draws nigh [eggizo].
8.notes: sterizo (G4741) is to prop a thing so it cannot tip: hearts shored up like vine-stakes for the long wait. eggizo (G1448), the drawing-near verb of 4:8 -- the God who came close to the humble is coming close to history; nearness is the church's load-bearing fact.

9.text: Do not groan against one another, brothers, so that you are not judged. Look -- the Judge is standing right at the doors.
9.amp: Grudge ['groan, grieve', stenazo, the KJV margin] not one against another [allelon], brethren [adelphos], lest you be condemned [katakrino]: behold [idou], the judge [krites] stands [histemi] before [pro] the door [thura].
9.notes: stenazo (G4727): not open quarreling but the low mutual groan of worn-out people -- pressure finds the nearest target, usually a brother. The deterrent is proximity: the krites is not en route but histemi, already standing, pro thura (G2374), at the doors (cf. Matthew 24:33).

10.text: Take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord, my brothers, as your pattern of suffering hardship and of long patience.
10.amp: Take [lambano], my brethren [adelphos], the prophets [prophetes], who have spoken [laleo] in the name [onoma] of the Lord [kurios], for an example [hupodeigma -- a pattern to copy] of suffering affliction [kakopatheia] and of patience [makrothumia].
10.notes: hupodeigma (G5262) is a tracing-pattern, a model set under the page. The prophetes (G4396) spoke in the Lord's onoma and suffered for the speaking -- proof that faithfulness and affliction ride together, and that makrothumia (G3115) has a long and honored pedigree (cf. Matthew 5:12).

11.text: See how we count as blessed those who endured. You have heard of the endurance of Job, and you have seen the end the Lord brought -- that the Lord is deeply compassionate, and full of tender mercy.
11.amp: Behold [idou], we count them happy [makarizo -- call them blessed] which endure [hupomeno]. You have heard [akouo] of the patience [hupomone] of Job [Iob], and have seen [eido] the end [telos] of the Lord [kurios]; that the Lord is very pitiful [polusplagchnos -- of much deep feeling, great-hearted], and of tender mercy [oiktirmon -- compassionate].
11.notes: Job's hupomone (G5281) was no serene silence -- he roared -- but he endured without letting go of God. The telos kurios (G5056) is the story's last chapter (cf. Job 42:10-17), where the verdict on God's character comes in: polusplagchnos (G4184), a word James may have coined, mercy from the deepest inward parts.

12.text: But above all things, my brothers, do not swear -- not by heaven, not by the earth, not by any other oath. Let your yes be yes and your no be no, so that you do not fall under judgment.
12.amp: But above [pro] all things [pas], my brethren [adelphos], swear [omnuo] not, neither by heaven [ouranos], neither by the earth [ge], neither by any other [allos] oath [horkos]: but let your yea [nai] be yea; and your nay [ou], nay; lest you fall [pipto] into condemnation [hupokrisis -- 'hypocrisy' in some copies; judgment].
12.notes: His Brother's teaching almost verbatim (cf. Matthew 5:34-37): the escalating oath-culture -- by heaven, by earth, by one's head -- existed to grade which promises really bound, and Christ abolished the grades. nai nai, ou ou (G3483): a plain word from a whole heart, the single tongue the whole letter has been after.

13.text: Is anyone among you suffering hardship? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing psalms.
13.amp: Is any among you afflicted [kakopatheo -- suffering hardship]? let him pray [proseuchomai]. Is any merry [euthumeo -- of good cheer]? let him sing psalms [psallo -- make music in praise].
13.notes: Both weathers get an upward channel: kakopatheo (G2553) into proseuchomai, euthumeo (G2114) into psallo (G5567). Neither pain nor gladness is to be spent horizontally on grumbling or self-congratulation -- the whole emotional range routed Godward.

14.text: Is anyone among you sick? Let him send for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the Lord's name;
14.amp: Is any sick [astheneo -- weak, infirm] among you? let him call [proskaleo] for the elders [presbuteros] of the church [ekklesia]; and let them pray [proseuchomai] over [epi] him, anointing [aleipho] him with oil [elaion] in the name [onoma] of the Lord [kurios]:
14.notes: The sick man calls; the presbuteroi (G4245) come -- the church's ministry moves to the bedside. aleipho (G218) with elaion (G1637) was both medicine and consecration in one act (cf. Mark 6:13); the power sits in neither the oil nor the office but in the onoma kurios that seals the prayer.

15.text: and the prayer offered in faith will save the sick man, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he has sins on his account, he will be forgiven them.
15.amp: And the prayer [euche] of faith [pistis] shall save [sozo] the sick [kamno -- the one worn down], and the Lord [kurios] shall raise him up [egeiro]; and if he have committed [poieo] sins [hamartia], they shall be forgiven [aphiemi] him.
15.notes: The subject is the euche pistis (G2171, G4102), and the actor is the kurios -- egeiro (G1453), the resurrection verb, doing bedside duty. The conditional 'if' guards against Job's-comforters logic: sickness is not proof of sin, but where sin is present, aphiemi (G863) travels with the healing; body and conscience rise together.

16.text: Confess your trespasses to one another, and pray for one another, so that you may be healed. The working prayer of a righteous man has great strength.
16.amp: Confess [exomologeo -- acknowledge openly] your faults [paraptoma -- trespasses] one to another [allelon], and pray [euchomai] one for another, that you may be healed [iaomai]. The effectual fervent [energeo -- inworking, operative] prayer [deesis] of a righteous man [dikaios] avails [ischuo -- is strong] much [polus].
16.notes: exomologeo (G1843) allelon: confession as ordinary congregational air, not crisis-only -- hidden paraptoma (G3900) block the healing that openness releases (iaomai, G2390). The famous clause: deesis energoumene (G1162, G1754), prayer with God's energy working in it, ischuo polus -- it is strong, and the dikaios praying need only be righteous, not rare, as verse 17 hurries to prove.

17.text: Elijah was a man of the same nature as we are, and he prayed earnestly -- prayed in his praying -- that it would not rain, and it did not rain on the land for three years and six months.
17.amp: Elias [Elias -- Elijah] was a man [anthropos] subject to like passions as we are ['of the same nature, a fellow mortal', homoiopathes, the KJV margin], and he prayed earnestly ['in his prayer', proseuche proseuchomai -- prayed with prayer, the Hebrew intensive] that it might not rain [brecho]: and it rained not on the earth [ge] by the space of three [treis] years [eniautos] and six [hex] months [men].
17.notes: homoiopathes (G3663): same nature, same passions -- the man who outran chariots also despaired under a broom tree (cf. 1 Kings 19:4). 'He prayed in his praying,' the doubled Hebrew idiom: whole-souled asking. The drought of 1 Kings 17-18, timed at three and a half years, hung on one mortal's prayer.

18.text: And he prayed again, and the sky gave rain, and the earth sprouted with her fruit.
18.amp: And he prayed [proseuchomai] again [palin], and the heaven [ouranos] gave [didomi] rain [huetos], and the earth [ge] brought forth [blastano -- sprouted, budded] her fruit [karpos].
18.notes: The Carmel sequel (cf. 1 Kings 18:42-45): bowed to the ground, seven times sending the servant to look. ouranos didomi -- the sky itself became a giver -- and blastano (G985), the sprouting, closes the loop with the farmer of verse 7: rain, fruit, and patience all answer to prayer.

19.text: My brothers, if anyone among you wanders from the truth and someone turns him back,
19.amp: Brethren [adelphos], if any of you do err [planao -- wander, be led astray] from the truth [aletheia], and one convert [epistrepho -- turn back] him;
19.notes: planao (G4105), the wandering-word of 1:16, now describing a brother drifting off the road of aletheia (G225) -- doctrine and conduct both, in this letter. epistrepho (G1994) is the shepherd's verb: one member going after one straggler.

20.text: let him know that the one who turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save a soul from death, and will cover a multitude of sins.
20.amp: Let him know [ginosko], that he which converts [epistrepho] the sinner [hamartolos] from the error [plane] of his way [hodos] shall save [sozo] a soul [psuche] from death [thanatos], and shall hide [kalupto -- cover] a multitude [plethos] of sins [hamartia].
20.notes: The letter ends mid-rescue, without a farewell: sozo psuche ek thanatos -- the very death that sin full-grown births in 1:15, prevented. kalupto (G2572) echoes Proverbs 10:12, love covering all wrongs: the recovered wanderer's sins go under the covering of forgiveness. James closes doing what he wrote the whole letter to do.
